tldr: This paper brings the physical priors of large-scale video generation models into mobile manipulation. By introducing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) that prevents interference between locomotion and manipulation, along with a training method (CoF) that autoregressively predicts future latent states, it achieves highly accurate and fast whole-body control without adding any inference cost.
hero_caption: An overview of MobileWAM. It integrates a pretrained video generation model with an action expert, training latent representations using future prediction (Chain-of-Foresight) during training only. At inference time, video generation is omitted for fast operation, achieving significantly higher success rates than existing methods in both simulation (ManiSkill-HAB) and on a real robot (ARX Lift2).
overview:
Mobile manipulation, where a robot moves around a room while manipulating objects, is an extremely challenging problem compared to tabletop manipulation. The camera viewpoint shifts dramatically, and locomotion and manipulation are intricately intertwined. Recently, applying world models (video diffusion models) trained on web-scale videos to robot manipulation has attracted significant attention, but prior work has remained confined to tabletop setups with fixed camera viewpoints.

To address this, the authors propose MobileWAM, bridging the rich physical motion priors of video generation models to mobile manipulation. To tackle the issue where moving and manipulating—two actions with heterogeneous dynamics—interfere with each other, they developed Mobile MoE, which splits feed-forward layers into three experts: Locomotion, Manipulation, and Shared. Furthermore, to capture long-term causal chains, they introduced Chain-of-Foresight (CoF), which sequentially predicts a chain of future latent states. Crucially, the foresight branch is discarded at deployment, and the model serves as a single feature encoder for the current image; thus, it runs at the same high speed as a standard policy without waiting for video generation.

In evaluations, MobileWAM recorded an average success rate of 73.0% across 7 tasks on the large-scale ManiSkill-HAB benchmark, surpassing existing SOTA methods that use point clouds or privileged information using only RGB images. Furthermore, when deployed on the real wheeled dual-arm mobile manipulator ARX Lift2, it outperformed a strong baseline ($\pi_{0.5}$) by a large margin on long-horizon tasks such as opening a drawer and stowing objects. This groundbreaking result shows that video world models can truly unleash their power in whole-body mobile robot coordination.
contributions: Systematically applied video diffusion models to whole-body mobile manipulation, updating the SOTA on ManiSkill-HAB in a single-stage training setup using RGB images only.

Proposed Chain-of-Foresight (CoF), a training method that autoregressively predicts future latent features in an RNN-like fashion to enhance long-horizon spatiotemporal and causal consistency without increasing inference cost at all.
Introduced Mobile MoE, which dynamically routes among locomotion, manipulation, and shared experts within the action model to prevent interference between motions with heterogeneous dynamics.
Implemented the method on the real mobile manipulator ARX Lift2, demonstrating that its advantage over a strong baseline ($\pi_{0.5}$) widens as task horizons grow longer.

sections.heading: Why mobile manipulation needs video world models
sections.summary: Mobile manipulation is not just a simple addition of 'locomotion + tabletop manipulation'; it is an inherently difficult problem where viewpoint changes, multimodality, and deep causal chains multiply. Solving these requires physical priors that anticipate how the world evolves, making video diffusion models a natural fit.
sections.details:
Three critical gaps exist between tabletop manipulation and mobile manipulation.

The first is 'Viewpoint'. In tabletop setups, cameras are fixed, but on a mobile robot, the camera moves drastically with the robot's own movement (ego-motion), demanding visual representations robust to egocentric viewpoint shifts.
The second is 'Multimodality'. Because the base can move, countless combinations of base and arm trajectories can achieve the same task goal, resulting in an extraordinarily complex action distribution.
The third is 'Causality'. A slight positioning error during the initial base movement will inevitably lead to a failure in subsequent grasping. In other words, the core difficulty lies in the 'causal depth' rather than just the number of steps.

Shallow image-to-action mappings such as conventional Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models cannot handle this complexity, leading previous studies to rely on 3D point clouds or privileged ground-truth segmentation. Meanwhile, video diffusion transformers pretrained on web-scale videos encapsulate rich physical laws and world dynamics, drawing attention as World Action Models (WAMs). However, prior studies have focused almost exclusively on stationary tabletop robots, failing to leverage the true strengths of video models. MobileWAM was proposed as a systematic architecture to bridge this gap.

sections.heading: The intersection of world action models and mobile manipulation
sections.summary: Existing world action models (WAMs) remain biased toward tabletop manipulation, while mobile manipulation research has relied on modular pipelines or special 3D representations and privileged information. MobileWAM unifies these by directly transferring video generation priors to whole-body control from RGB images alone.
sections.details:
The positioning of this work lies at the intersection of three main research threads.

- The trend of World Action Models (WAMs):
These models acquire physical representations by generatively imagining future observations. While early approaches were two-stage pipelines separating video generation from action generation, recent methods like Motus and LingBot-VA unify them within a single diffusion transformer. However, all of these assume stationary tabletop setups.

- Mobile manipulation approaches:
Modular approaches that decouple navigation from manipulation suffer from error accumulation across stages. On the other hand, end-to-end imitation learning (such as the $\pi_0$ family and AC-DiT) tackles whole-body coordination, but predominantly requires 3D point cloud inputs or privileged auxiliary supervision such as ground-truth object masks. MobileWAM eliminates these complex human-crafted pipelines, achieving consistency from RGB inputs alone through the power of a pretrained video model.

- Future prediction as an auxiliary task:
An approach that strengthens representation learning by predicting future latent features instead of generating raw pixels. While inspired by next-token prediction and Next-Latent Prediction in LLMs, MobileWAM's Chain-of-Foresight (CoF) is unique in that it 'recursively chains the temporal evolution of the physical world'.

sections.heading: Architecture of MobileWAM: whole-body control via MoE and foresight chains
sections.summary: A video diffusion model (World Expert) and an action generation model (Action Expert) are integrated through layerwise joint attention. Incorporating a three-expert Mobile MoE that prevents interference between moving and manipulating, as well as CoF that sequentially predicts future latent states, the model operates ultra-fast at inference by caching current features.
sections.details:
MobileWAM consists of the following components:

3.1 Overview and Input/Output:
At time step $t$, the model takes two RGB camera views (head and wrist), proprioception $\bm{s}_t$ (an 18-dimensional vector of joint positions, velocities, and odometry), and a language instruction $\ell$. The output is a whole-body action chunk $\bm{a}_{t:t+H}$ spanning $H=4$ steps, commanding a total of 13 dimensions simultaneously: arm (7-DoF), gripper, head pan-tilt, lift torso, and base velocity.

3.2 World Expert (Video Backbone):
It adopts a pretrained Wan video diffusion transformer (30 blocks, hidden size 3072). It is compressed $4\times$ temporally by a 3D VAE, so 1 latent step perfectly matches the action chunk length ($H=4$). The head and wrist camera images are concatenated horizontally, naturally preserving cross-view consistency through attention.

3.3 Action Expert and Mobile MoE:
The action side is a lightweight transformer with a hidden dimension of 1024. Across all 30 layers, visual tokens from the video side and action tokens undergo layerwise joint attention. A key innovation here is 'Mobile MoE'. When controlling base movement across space and delicate arm manipulation requiring fine contact using shared weights, their gradients cause destructive interference. Therefore, every FFN layer in the action model is partitioned into three experts: Shared, Locomotion, and Manipulation. A soft router weights them based on motion intent extracted from the action tokens, achieving specialization without interference.

3.4 Chain-of-Foresight (CoF):
To teach the model long-term causal chains—not just 'what happens next?' but 'what happens after that, and after that?'—features are extracted from 4 backbone layers (layers 4, 12, 20, and 30) to recursively predict future latent states $\bm{z}_1, \dots, \bm{z}_K$ like an RNN. The belief state $\bm{h}_k$ at each step passes the world state forward to the next step.

3.5 Attention Mask and Inference Efficiency:
An asymmetric attention mask is used: video tokens do not attend to action tokens, and action tokens attend only to current observation tokens. As a result, video generation and CoF computation are completely discarded at deployment. By caching the backbone output of the current image just once, iterative action denoising can run rapidly, achieving a $5\times$ to $8\times$ speedup compared to conventional video-generating WAMs.

(b) Chain-of-Foresight (CoF), which functions only during training, predicts a chain of future latent states. (c) The structure of Mobile MoE, dynamically routing between locomotion, manipulation, and shared experts based on action intent.

sections.heading: Outstanding performance and generalization validated in simulation and real-world experiments
sections.summary: MobileWAM achieved an average success rate of 73.0% on the ManiSkill-HAB benchmark, substantially surpassing existing SOTA methods. Ablations confirmed the effectiveness of both CoF and MoE designs, and real-world household tasks on the ARX Lift2 robot showed that it outperformed the baseline ($\pi_{0.5}$) across all tasks.
sections.details:
4.1 Experimental Setup:
Simulation was evaluated on 7 tasks from the ManiSkill-HAB (SetTable) household rearrangement benchmark using a Fetch robot. Training was done in a single stage using 1,000 demonstration trajectories per task. The input is RGB images only, without using depth or point clouds.

4.2 Comparison with SOTA:
In Table 1, MobileWAM achieved an average success rate of 73.0%, leading all baseline methods by a wide margin (AnchorVLA at 64.0%, AC-DiT at 55.6%, RDT at 42.9%, etc.). It earned the top score on 5 out of 7 tasks, including difficult tasks where other methods nearly collapsed toward zero.

4.3 Ablation Studies:
- Component effects (Table 2): Adding CoF to the base WAM (65.4%) improved performance to 68.9% (+3.5 points), and further adding Mobile MoE raised it to 73.0% (+4.1 points), steadily stacking gains.
- Parallel prediction vs. sequential chain (Table 3): Simply predicting the future in parallel achieved only 52.3%, but chaining it autoregressively with a transformer as in CoF surged to 58.2% (under a reduced budget of 5,000 steps). This proves the importance of chaining causal dependencies step by step.
- MoE design (Table 6): Hard-partitioning locomotion and manipulation into completely separate networks degraded performance. An MoE that softly divides roles while retaining shared representations performed the best.

4.4 Inference Speed and Real-Robot Deployment:
Inference time is approximately 938 ms per cycle, which is $5\times$ to $8\times$ faster than Motus (~5.0 s) or LingBot-VA (~8.2 s) that generate full videos before acting (Table 7). In 5 household tasks ($T_a$ through $T_e$) using the real ARX Lift2 robot, MobileWAM outperformed the recent $\pi_{0.5}$ across all tasks (Table 8). In particular, on the longest compound task $T_e$ ('open drawer, pick object from shelf, place in drawer, and close drawer'), $\pi_{0.5}$ had a 0% success rate, whereas MobileWAM achieved 15%, demonstrating its strength in long-horizon causal tasks.

4.5 Failure Analysis:
Roughly 40% of failures were fine positioning errors (falling outside tolerances for grasping or placing), and about 25% were unintended collisions. Failures occurred frequently near the boundaries of the arm's reachable workspace, highlighting geometric precision as a future challenge.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future directions
sections.summary: MobileWAM establishes a powerful framework for adapting video generation priors to mobile manipulation. By eliminating motion interference via MoE and learning causality via CoF, it significantly boosts whole-body coordination performance without any added inference cost.
sections.details:
This study represents a pioneering effort in fully integrating video generation world models into mobile manipulation. Grounded on three pillars—fusing video and actions through layerwise joint attention, Mobile MoE reconciling locomotion and manipulation, and Chain-of-Foresight introducing zero runtime overhead—it achieves top-tier performance through a simple, single-stage training pipeline relying strictly on RGB images.

Promising future directions highlighted by the authors include post-training with reinforcement learning or human intervention data, incorporating geometric information beyond RGB, and integrating CoF directly into the large-scale pretraining stage of video models. The authors conclude that 'mobile manipulation is where world action models belong and can unleash their true potential.'

sections.heading: Appendix: implementation details and behind the scenes of real-world and simulated setups
sections.summary: Provides model parameters, loss weighting, and detailed experimental protocols for the real ARX Lift2 and the ManiSkill-HAB simulator. It details real-world deployment via Wi-Fi remote GPU inference and routing analysis showing that the MoE router aligns cleanly with actual base and arm velocities.
sections.details:
The appendix includes critical details beneficial for reproducibility and real-world deployment.

- Implementation and Optimization Parameters:
The video backbone is roughly 6.5B parameters (Wan-based, 30 blocks, hidden size 3072), with its VAE and T5 text encoder frozen. The action side has 30 blocks and a hidden size of 1024. Flow Matching loss weights are set to 1.0 for both video and action, CoF weight is $\lambda=0.1$, and depth-decaying weights $\bm{w}=(0.4, 0.2, 0.1)$ are applied (chain length $K=3$).

- Real-World Robot Setup (ARX Lift2):
The robot features a wheeled mobile base, a lift torso, and a single arm. Because its onboard PC cannot host large models, it communicates over Wi-Fi with an external server equipped with two NVIDIA A800 GPUs, executing remote inference with a cycle of approximately 938 ms from sending images to receiving action chunks.

- Routing Analysis of Mobile MoE (Figure S8):
Analyzing the trained router weights reveals that during phases dominated by base velocity, the 'Locomotion expert' weight automatically increases, whereas during arm-dominant phases, the 'Manipulation expert' is chosen. Even without an explicit regularization loss, a desirable division of roles emerges naturally according to motion intent.

captions.F8: The 5 evaluation tasks ($T_a$ through $T_e$) on the real ARX Lift2 robot. The robot executes smoothly with egocentric viewpoint shifts across tasks ranging from opening and closing drawers to complex, long-horizon sequences spanning shelves and drawers.

takeaways: The rich physical priors of video generation models unleash their true value in mobile manipulation, where viewpoints shift drastically and causal relationships run deep.

When learning degrees of freedom with heterogeneous dynamics (locomotion and manipulation) end-to-end, splitting feed-forward layers via MoE prevents interference and substantially boosts performance.

Chain-of-Foresight, which autoregressively predicts future latent representations in an RNN fashion only during training, is an exceptional training technique for acquiring long-term consistency without adding a single millisecond to inference.

Leveraging asymmetric attention and caching the current frame allows policies to exploit the heavy priors of video models while achieving a millisecond-level control loop practical for real-world deployment.
limitations: Small positioning errors tend to occur near the robot's workspace boundaries (limits of reachable range), serving as the primary cause of grasping and placement failures.
Because it currently relies solely on RGB images, there are limitations in guaranteeing strict geometric consistency, such as millimeter-precision contacts or avoiding thin obstacles.

With approximately 6.5B parameters, the model cannot run real-time inference on the robot's onboard computer and relies on high-speed Wi-Fi communication with a powerful external GPU server such as an A800.
